questions.q: Why does the capstone start by stating a clear business question before writing any PySpark code?
options: It has no real effect on the pipeline's design
Business questions are only relevant for pandas pipelines, not PySpark
PySpark requires a written question as a code comment before it will run
A real pipeline exists to answer a specific question, and stating it first gives you a way to check whether the finished pipeline actually did its job
questions.explain: Writing the goal down first turns the pipeline from an abstract exercise into something checkable against a real target.

questions.q: Why does the clean() step filter out rows with fare_amount <= 0 or trip_distance <= 0?
options: Spark cannot process negative numbers at all
Filtering them out is only cosmetic and has no effect on the result
Those rows are always duplicates of other rows
Those records (refunds, void trips, data errors) would quietly skew an average-fare calculation toward meaningless numbers
questions.explain: Trusting every raw record, including obviously invalid ones, would corrupt the final aggregation.

questions.q: In the transform() step, what does logging a warning for trips with no matching pickup zone accomplish?
options: It has no effect since the join already guarantees a match
It automatically removes those rows from the DataFrame
It stops the pipeline from running any further
It surfaces a potential data quality issue instead of letting unmatched rows pass through silently unnoticed
questions.explain: A left join can produce nulls for the zone columns, and logging that count makes the issue visible rather than hidden.

questions.q: Why filter out pickup zones with fewer than 50 trips before ranking by average fare?
options: It has no effect on which zones appear in the final result
It is required to avoid a divide-by-zero error
A zone with very few trips and one unusually expensive fare could misleadingly appear at the top of the ranking
PySpark cannot aggregate groups with fewer than 50 rows
questions.explain: This is a real judgment call data engineers make to keep an aggregation meaningful, not just mechanically correct.

questions.q: Why split the pipeline into small, named functions (extract, clean, transform, aggregate, load) instead of one long script?
options: It makes the pipeline run on more CPU cores automatically
Each piece can be checked and tested independently, which is exactly what makes Lesson 48's validation step possible
It has no practical benefit over a single long script
PySpark requires every pipeline to be split into exactly five functions
questions.explain: This mirrors Chapter 6's ETL design principles, and isolating each stage is what allows targeted validation afterward.
